taxonomyNote: Formerly Eumeces skiltonianus (still used in some sources, including the Montana Field Guide text and the Zion NPS key); Montana notes the southern Baja form is sometimes treated as a separate species.
fieldMarks: Slender, long-bodied lizard with smooth, shiny scales and a tail about as long as the body; adults about 5-8 cm snout-vent, up to 19 cm total.
Brown, black and cream/golden-yellow longitudinal stripes from the nose onto the tail; belly light gray to cream.
Young and young adults have a brilliant blue tail that fades with age.
Males develop reddish-orange on the chin and sides of the head in the breeding season; tail may be stumpy after loss.
behavior: Secretive; shelters under rocks, leaves and logs and digs burrows; inactive in cold winter weather.
Eats crickets, beetles, grasshoppers, flies, spiders and earthworms.
In Utah mates May-June and lays eggs in July (clutch 2-6, up to 10); the female guards eggs and stays with hatchlings.
habitat: Grassland, chaparral, open juniper-sage shrubland, pinyon-juniper, pine-oak and mixed conifer forest.
Favours grassy openings and rocky areas near streams and dry shaded hillsides.
range: Western North America from south-central British Columbia to northwestern Baja California, from the Pacific coast east to western Montana, Idaho, eastern Utah and north-central Arizona, to about 2,530 m.

lookalikes.name: Western fence lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Keeled, prickly scales and never a blue tail.

lookalikes.name: Northern alligator lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Has a skin fold on the side of the body and short legs.
